summary: This is the finished House class: it stores an address, a bedroom count, and a bathroom count, exposes getters and setters for each, and adds a toString method so a House can be printed as readable text instead of a memory address.

lines.text: The fields are marked private so that outside code cannot reach in and change them directly; every change must go through a method the class controls.

lines.code: public House(String address, int bedrooms, double bathrooms) {
lines.text: The constructor demands all three values up front, so it is impossible to create a House that is missing its address or room counts.
The parameter and the field share the name address, so this.address makes it clear that the field is being assigned from the parameter.
Bathrooms is a double rather than an int because half baths are real: a house can have 2.5 bathrooms.
A getter hands out the stored value without exposing the field itself, which is the standard way to read private data.
A setter is the single doorway for changing the field later, which is where validation would go if you needed it.
This annotation tells the compiler you intend to replace a method inherited from Object; if you misspell the method name, compilation fails instead of silently doing nothing.
Every object inherits toString from Object, and Java calls it automatically whenever an object is printed or joined to a String, so defining it here controls how a House appears.
The return value is built by concatenating literal text with the field values, producing one line that names the class and lists its state.
The escaped '\'' is a single-quote character, wrapping the address in quotes so an empty or padded address is still visible in the output.
An int joined to a String is converted to its digits automatically, so no extra conversion call is needed.
